Slow-Roasted Tomatoes

British · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The tomato given time: halved, seasoned, and roasted at low heat for three-quarters of an hour until the flesh concentrates into something between a vegetable and a preserve — deeply sweet, faintly smoky at the edges, its juices reduced to a syrup in the cavity. This is the Sunday version of the grilled tomato and the make-ahead version of them all: a tray of slow-roasted tomatoes made once feeds four breakfasts, improves in the fridge, and turns a weekday plate into one that tastes like it had all morning. The technique is low-and-long: 150 °C dries and concentrates without burning, the sugar develops slowly, and the only judgement is the pull point — slumped and syrupy, not dried and leathery. Winter tomatoes, which the high-heat methods punish, become honest food here.

  • ripe ones if the season allows; respectable ones otherwise, because the method forgives

  • they roast sweet in their skins and squeeze out over the finished tomato)
- **Low heat is the method's spine:** 150 °C (fan 130 °C). The temperature dries the flesh slowly enough for its sugars to concentrate without caramelising to bitterness — the exact opposite logic of the pan-fried tomato's hot-and-fast sear, and the two dishes prove the same vegetable has two honest destinations. - **Salt and drain 10 minutes first**, blot, then season — the standard move, and at this long a roast it matters even more: water left in the flesh steams the first 20 minutes and delays the concentration. - **One tray, cut-face up, well-spaced** — the halves' juices reduce in their own cavities; crowding steams them together into a compote. Lovely, but a different dish.

Slow-Roasted Tomatoes

Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 45 minutes · Total: 50 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

The tomatoes

  • 8 medium vine tomatoes (800 g), halved through the equator — ripe ones if the season allows; respectable ones otherwise, because the method forgives

The seasoning

  • 30 ml / 28 g olive oil
  • 4 g fine sea salt
  • 2 g soft light brown sugar
  • 2 g black pepper
  • 4 sprigs fresh thyme (or 2 g dried)
  • 2 garlic cloves, skin-on, smashed (optional — they roast sweet in their skins and squeeze out over the finished tomato)

Instructions

  1. **Season and load.** After the salt-drain and blot, arrange the halves cut-face up on the tray. Drizzle the oil over, then the sugar, pepper, and a final light salt; tuck the thyme sprigs and garlic between the halves. Checkpoint — each cavity holds a small pool of seasoned oil, the cut faces are matte and dry, and the seasoning sits where the roasting will concentrate it. Crowded halves get their own second tray — space is an ingredient here.
  2. **Roast at 150 °C, 45 minutes.** Into the oven, middle shelf. At 25 minutes, check once: the edges should be beginning to wrinkle and the cavities to deepen. At 45 minutes, pull them when the flesh has slumped by about a third, the edges are lightly caramelised, and the cavity juices have thickened to a syrup that coats a spoon. Checkpoint — the tomato is deeply slumped, glossy, and dense — a spoon lifts a half whole, and its cavity holds syrup, not water. The edges are bronzed, never black. If the cavities still swim at 45 minutes, give 10 more; if the edges have gone dark at 35, the oven runs hot — drop 10 °C.
  3. **Rest in the tray, 10 minutes.** Out of the oven and left on the tray — the halves reabsorb a little of their syrup as they cool, and the garlic squeezes from its skins over them if using. Checkpoint — the tomatoes are warm-not-hot, glossy with their own syrup, and hold their shape when lifted. Serve now, or cool completely and refrigerate — they are better on day two, which almost no breakfast component can claim.
  4. **Land — hot on the plate, or from the fridge re-warmed.** For the Sunday plate, spoon the syrup over them and serve beside the eggs. For the weekday, re-warm 4–5 halves on a tray at 160 °C for 8 minutes. Checkpoint — the eating test: a spoonful that tastes of tomato intensified — sweet, salted, faintly thymic — with a yielding jam texture and none of the raw acidity the fresh tomato carries. It is the grilled tomato's flavour, multiplied.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Still watery at 45 minutesOven cool or tray crowdedVerify 150 °C; space the halves; give 10–15 more minutes
Leathery, dried-out halvesOver-roasted or too hotPull at the slumped-syrup stage; 140 °C for a longer run next time
Bitter edgesOven hot or sugar skippedThe 150 °C check; the sugar buffers the caramelisation
Bland resultUnder-salted or unripe tomatoes, uncorrectedSalt up at the end; a final squeeze of lemon lifts a flat tray

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **The best-keeping tomato on the site:** 1 week refrigerated under a film of their oil, 3 months frozen, and — potted in sterilised jars with fresh oil — the beginnings of a preserve. They improve for 2–3 days in the fridge. - **Variation — the balsamic version:** 10 ml balsamic drizzled in the last 10 minutes — the supper-cousin, as good with the gammon steak as with breakfast. - **Variation — the chilli version:** a pinch of chilli flakes with the seasoning — the bean-pot's friend. - **The trio completed:** grilled (fast, jammy, element), pan-fried (faster, crusty, fat), slow-roasted (slowest, concentrated, make-ahead) — the fry-up's tomato doctrine in three records, one vegetable, no wrong answers.
